The last mission truly was one of my favourites. It plays out like an interactive cutscene, and I could not get enough of the pure adrenaline and tension it was giving me. I can only hope for someone to see this game's potential and create a sequel one day. 
Anyway long story short, I could rant on about the intricacies and details of every mission in this game for hours; I could write a whole essay on how it made me feel and how much I love it. But to keep it semi-short: buy this game. It is a masterpiece, and you will not regret it.

Some people will love Alien: Isolation and some people will hate it. This game really succeeds at ramping up the tension in a way that few other games can match. It's a genuine horror experience. But if you're looking for something that's "fun" in the conventional sense, stay far away from this one. I will recommend it as long as you know what you're getting into. For the right kind of horror fan, this game should be a 10/10. But be warned - this game is not for everyone.

I have to praise the atmosphere. The environments are very reminiscent of the film series, and they are fun to explore. The game is a few years old as of 2017, so the graphics are no longer top-of-the-line, but they are good enough to make the experience feel immersive. The sound design is even better, and might be the best part of the game. I highly recommend wearing your best headphones while playing. You will have to constantly listen for sound cues to see if you're in danger. You're on a space station that is noisy and creaky, and it will mess with your head. Good stuff.

The Alien itself is great. It looks just like it does in the movies. It is powerful, it is fast, and it wants you dead. The AI isn't perfect, but it definitely achieves its main goal: it forces you to stay on your toes at all times. This creature is as terrifying as a video game character can be.

Unfortunately, the tension in this game comes at a cost. Part of the reason you will be so scared to die in this game is that the save points are far apart, so every time you die it's a significant setback. If you get stuck on one part of the game, you might have to play the same 15 minutes over and over. This does help to make the game feel scary, but if that feeling wears off then it just becomes annoying and tedious. I'm playing it on the "normal" difficulty level, and honestly I wish I had picked a lower one because I just want to see more of the game instead of having a burdensome death knocking on my door at all times.

As you progress, the game starts to get repetitive, and the pace of it gets really slow. No matter where you go, the Alien is always nearby. To avoid him you have to find hiding places. So, you sit in a closet and wait around for a few minutes until he backs off. Then you sneak past him so you can find the next closet to hide in. And unfortunately, that is most of the gameplay. So if you ever get tired of hiding in closets and under tables, you will start to hate this game. Alien: Isolation may look like an FPS, but it rarely plays like an FPS. Do not try to fight the Alien, unless you want to see him kill you. Don't fire your gun anywhere near him, because he can hear gunshots and he will come looking for you.

Let's see...what else is there? The story is alright. I like how it fits into the lore of the series, but it never really gets me to care about the characters. The main character is a tough lady engineer - appropriate for the part but nothing special. There are humans and synthetic androids hanging around occasionally, most of which are hostile so you usually just avoid them. The controls are good. I played mostly with a keyboard and mouse, but I also tried an Xbox controller. They are both basically fine. A mouse lets you turn around faster, and a controller lets you peek around corners more carefully. There is a crafting system. I am sick of every game having a crafting system, so I didn't get much out of that, but it is at least functional. I haven't played any of the DLC yet, so I won't comment on that.

So if that a really tense game sounds good to you, then give it a try. If you're not sure and just want to try it, then wait until it's on sale and play on a low difficulty level.

I feel a bit silly adding a review to a game that has been tried and played and reviewed to death over the past four years or so. But the thing is, I only recently played this game for the first time. I'm an older gamer - in my forties, and therefore old enough to have been terrified by Ridley Scott's original Alien movie when it first hit the screen. this may or may not have a bearing on the fact that I find this game amazing. If you sit down to play it (preferably alone, in a dark room, on a dark night), and immerse yourself in it, you can let the sound and atmosphere of the whole thing draw you in gradually.

A bit like in the original  film, the alien itself - as in the graphics and effects of the actual complete xenomorph creature, are not quite as horrifying as the tension and suspense surrounding it. But the game here is precisely about that tension and suspense. As you go about your various tasks, you are being hunted down, by the game's artificial intelligence. If this thing finds you, you will not survive. But all the time it doesn't hear you or see you, it is possible to outsmart and out-manouvre it. Some mechanics in the game make this a strategic thing - for example, you are given a "proximity detector" - a device which lets you see where the alien is in relation to you, within a certain scope. But this gadget itself makes a noise, so if the alien is too close, it'll hear you using it, and come for light snack.

Don't expect rushing around blasting things. expect creeping around avoiding things, and trying to STFU.

I highly recommend this game to anyone that knows the ALIEN movie and hasn't tried this game. It captures the spirit and tone of Ridley Scott's vision better than any of the Alien movies they made after the first 2. Theyve made an online series of the cut scenes. Maybe they should make it into a TV series. Nearly five years after release, it still stands strong as an adventure worth immersing yourself in.

The center of gravity of the story lies in the events on the Sevastopol space station, where an alien appears fifteen years after the end of the first film - and chaos breaks out. With mechanic Amanda Ripley (Ellen's daughter from the film series), you have to survive him, and in addition to the title enemy, you also face wild people and androids, controlled by the central artificial intelligence of Apollo.

The crucial fact is that Alien Isolation will not collapse in the shooter after a few hours. There are many enemies to fire, but Amanda feels good with a plasma torch, not a shotgun. This also ends the similarity of digital DNA to System Shock or Dead Space games, in which the set-up and content were similar, but the point lay in the clever setting of enemies. Isolation is simply not an action RPG. This is a successful stealth experiment, where the uncompromising rule of "not being seen" means surviving. As for the understanding of this experiment, it is good to keep in mind that this is not an adaptation of Aliens (directed by James Cameron), but Alien (a thriller under the baton of Ridley Scott). And it's not a game about an alien either, but with an alien. These are the big differences that play a crucial role.

The one alien you come across is indestructible. By their behavior, they push you into stealthy movement, crawling through ventilation shafts and waiting under the table or in cupboards. With a slow and careful movement, the hours of playing fulfill the term thriller, ie stretching the nerves to the brim. These are long corridors with one b*tch. You will spend infinitely long minutes watching the motion detector, on which a green dot pulsates, and decide whether the passage of the rooms is safe or the alien will return suddenly.
You have to be extremely careful when moving. The murderous beast reacts to sounds even from a great distance and, unlike human or android opponents, you will not escape it. All you have to do is run around the metal floor, refrain from hacking the terminal, cutting through the hatches or opening the hydraulic door, and a bang will sound around the corner, announcing that the alien has just jumped to your floor through the air conditioning outlet. A moment of delay? Death.

The stealth game does not make the film Alien a shame and will be enjoyed by a fan of the series as well as an uninterested player. [b] 65% [/b]

Alien Isolation is a game where you die a lot. It is probably my favorite Game Over screen simulator to this date. This being said, the repeated deaths and constant restarts do not distract from the overall experience (other than making the One Shot achievement altogether impossible). While they are upsetting, they do a fine job in restoring a bit of honor to the franchise after Colonial Marines angrily flogged the once-terrifying Xenomorph repeatedly in the behind with a ruler. The Alien is scary again.

Alien Isolation understands what few horror games understand nowadays. Being weak is scary. Running through a shopping mall blasting zombies in the face with an endless arsenal of over-the-top weapons is not scary. Having to constantly worry about running out of ammo, and having to check around each corner before slowly moving ahead with the constant threat of an unseen enemy hanging over your head is scary.

And Alien Isolation does that well. Because you will die. A lot.

The design of Sevastopol Station is amazing, and is able to keep you on somewhat a linear pathway so that you feel like you are still progressing (although slowly with the constant threat of death just around every corner) without making you feel confined to a small world. It still feels open and full of possible discoveries (that perhaps you will come back to later since you are probably about to die and seeing what's inside that box isn't worth restarting the past half hour).

The sound design is terrifying. The sound of the Alien's heavy footsteps in the air vents, the angry yelling (and good voice acting, including some of the original cast members) of survivors (who want you dead just like everything else on the ship), the hiss of an Alien that has just spotted you hiding in that locker, and the eerie creak of the entire ship slowly tearing itself apart.

The main attraction is clearly the Alien itself. It looks amazing. It looks scary. It's big and smart and feels real. The AI is smarter than you sometimes and would've put the AI in Colonial Marines to shame even if it had been all that had been promised before release. It learns from your actions, and something that may have worked last time may not work the next time because it saw you get away with it last time.

This AI actually works very well with the story, which is equally impressive. For such an expansive franchise, such as the Alien franchise, it is easy for a developer to just create new cannon-fodder characters and throw them in a world that feels familiar to the franchise world we're familiar with, and call it an official part of the storyline by slapping a label on it. But Creative Assembly actually put thought into this, and made it work with the gameplay. You are a character you care about. *Some of* the characters who die felt like genuine people who you wish would've made it. This makes for an intriguing story, and it revolves around a gap in the official storyline that actually makes the story feel more complete, instead of just like cannon-fodder.

This combination of great story-telling, genuine scary gameplay, and impressive sound/art design makes for a game worthy of the Alien franchise. This is truly the Alien game we've waited for, and it repents of all of Colonial Marines' previous sins.
